Monday. Saurabh spread three sheets on the floor of his room and drew the site by hand: a home page with his name and one line about what he builds, three project pages, a contact block. On each project page he drew four boxes and labelled them: problem, my part, result, link.
Wednesday. He showed the sketches to Gurleen, who circled the "result" box on the first project. "This one is empty," she said. "Then I need a real number," Saurabh replied, and wrote himself a note.
Saturday. He opened the editor. Because every page already had its shape, he finished the home page and the first project page before dinner, and did not once wonder what to put next.

qa.q: What four boxes did Saurabh draw on each project page?
qa.a: He labelled the boxes problem, my part, result and link.

qa.q: What is Saurabh probably feeling on Saturday evening?
qa.a: Saurabh is probably satisfied and steady, since he finished two pages before dinner without wondering what came next.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Saurabh use if the design still feels vague, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could copy the structure of one portfolio he likes and change the content, because a structure that already works removes guessing about layout.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the sketches?
qa.a: Gurleen looks closely and circles the empty result box, so Gurleen sees the plan as useful and points out the missing piece before any code exists.

grounding: Shows sketching a portfolio site on paper and deciding what each project page must contain before coding.

subtype: Approach: storyboarding the portfolio site on paper [Action]
passage:
Zainab, before you open that laptop, let me, Lavanya, tell you how I made my first portfolio site, back when I was finishing my degree. I opened the code editor first and lost three evenings arguing with myself over a menu bar.
Then my hostel senior, Rukhsana, took my laptop away and handed me a notebook. 'Draw it,' she said. So I drew a home page with one line about me and three project boxes. I drew a page for each project, and a small contact section at the bottom.
Drawing the project pages, I kept asking what a stranger would want to know. I ended up writing four headings on every page: the problem, my part, what happened, and a link.
After that the coding took two evenings, because I was only copying my drawings. Now take a pencil. Mine is in that drawer.

qa.q: What did Rukhsana hand Lavanya instead of the laptop?
qa.a: A notebook, with the words 'Draw it.'

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling during the three evenings spent on the menu bar?
qa.a: Lavanya felt stuck and frustrated, arguing over small details before knowing what the site needed.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how the site got built?
qa.a: Rukhsana taking the laptop away and asking for drawings first; once the pages and four headings were planned, coding took only two evenings.

qa.q: How might Rukhsana have seen those three lost evenings?
qa.a: Rukhsana likely saw a junior stuck on small details and knew a quick sketch would give the work a shape.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling sketching a portfolio's home, project and contact pages on paper and deciding every project page needs the problem, the part played, the result and a link.

subtype: Approach: storyboarding the portfolio site on paper [Action]
passage:
Hansa's laptop was at the repair shop for a week, and the campus placement portal wanted a portfolio link by the following Monday. On the overnight train home to Ludhiana, with only a notebook and a pen, she decided to plan instead of panic.
She drew the home page first: her name, one sentence about the work she liked, and three boxes for projects. Then one page per project. In each she wrote the same four questions: What problem? What did I do? What changed? Where can someone see it? The contact section went at the bottom, with just an email and a line inviting messages.
Gurleen, her friend in the next berth, woke at six and flipped through it. 'You've already built the whole site.'
'Just the drawings.'
On Friday the laptop came back. The site went up on Saturday, in one sitting.

qa.q: When did the laptop come back?
qa.a: On Friday the laptop came back.

qa.q: How was Hansa feeling on the train, and what did she do about it?
qa.a: She was likely anxious about the Monday deadline with no laptop, and chose to plan on paper instead of panicking.

qa.q: What else could Hansa do before the site goes live?
qa.a: Show the drawings to a senior who has been placed and ask whether the four questions come through clearly on each project page.

qa.q: What does the notebook show Gurleen at six in the morning?
qa.a: To Gurleen it looks as if the whole site already exists, which shows how much of the work the planning did.

grounding: Shows a student with no laptop sketching the home page, project pages and contact section on paper, with the same four questions for every project.
